controls.name: TLS between CI platform and Event Receiver
controls.description: Deployment events are sent from the external CI platform to the Event Receiver over HTTPS, so events on data flow df-001 are encrypted in transit between the CI platform and the notifier service.
limitations: TLS protects deployment events in transit on df-001 but does not authenticate the sender; the Event Receiver still accepts any well-formed JSON without verifying a CI signature.

mappings.applicability_reason: The threat involves a public Event Receiver and a Chat Notifier that relay deployment events to an internal chat channel for engineers, and no administrative or operator interface acting on customer data is described, so the requirement’s conditions for an administrative interface do not hold for this threat path.
No AI or machine-learning model is described for the Event Receiver, Chat Notifier, or Chat platform, so the conditions about passing untrusted content into a model do not hold for this threat.

The system under this threat does not use a model or publish model output; it only forwards deployment events to an internal chat channel, so the conditions about publishing model output externally do not hold.

No customer content is sent to an external model provider; the only external interaction is the CI platform posting deployment events and the notifier calling a chat API, so the requirement about data sent to an external model provider does not bear on this threat.
No AI model output is rendered into a user interface; the notifier constructs simple deployment messages for an internal chat channel, so the conditions for model-output encoding do not hold.

The threat path involves an external CI platform calling a public webhook and a service posting to an internal chat channel; there is no user-facing authentication delegated to an external identity provider in scope, so the requirement about documenting delegated user authentication does not bear on this threat.

No privileged administrative interface is described; the Event Receiver and Chat Notifier automatically forward deployment events and do not provide interactive administrative access, so the requirement about multi-factor authentication for privileged access does not apply to this threat.

The deploy notifier is described as an internal tool for engineers with no mention of multiple customers or organizations, so the conditions about multi-tenant data stored in shared storage do not hold for this threat.

While the notifier calls a chat platform API, it does so to post to an internal engineering chat channel rather than acting on customer resources on a customer’s behalf, so the requirement about limiting delegated integration privileges for customer resources does not bear on this threat.

This threat targets runtime handling of inbound deployment webhooks and chat notifications; the documentation does not describe the notifier’s own build or deployment pipeline, and the attack path does not involve pipeline authentication or third-party build components, so the CI/CD trust requirement does not bear on this specific spoofed-webhook threat.

Deployment events and notifications contain only repository names, environments, and commit identifiers, and the documentation states that no customer data passes through the notifier, so the path affected by this threat does not store or transmit sensitive customer data and the encryption requirement for sensitive data is not engaged.

The system is described as relaying deployment events that do not contain customer data, so the requirement about defining and enforcing retention for sensitive customer working data does not apply to this threat.

There is no description of stored customer artifacts or multi-tenant artifact storage; the notifier processes transient deployment events for internal engineers, so the requirement about tenant separation for stored artifacts does not bear on this threat.

The documentation states that no customer data passes through the notifier, so the requirement about deleting stored customer data on request does not apply to the components and assets involved in this threat.
Because the notifier handles only deployment metadata and explicitly no customer data, the requirement to exclude sensitive data from application logs is not engaged by this threat.

No administrative or privileged interface is described; the Event Receiver and Chat Notifier automatically process deployment events and do not expose operator actions on customer data or security configuration, so the requirement for auditing administrative actions does not bear on this threat.

The Event Receiver is explicitly documented as a public HTTPS endpoint called by the external CI platform, so for this threat it is a public interface by design rather than an internal data store, queue, cache, or internal service, and the internal-component network-reachability requirement does not apply.

The described attack sends forged HTTP POSTs directly to the public Event Receiver URL and does not depend on any long-lived signing keys or provider API credentials held by this system, so the requirement about storing such credentials in a managed secret store does not bear on this specific threat.

The threat scenario does not involve the system obtaining access to customer resources on an external platform via tokens; it concerns unauthenticated webhook deliveries to the Event Receiver, so the requirement about using short-lived credentials for customer resources is not engaged.

Although the notifier calls an external chat platform API, the documentation states that no customer data passes through the notifier, so the requirement about documenting external processor handling of customer data does not apply to this threat path.

Processing triggered by inbound deployment events consists of parsing a small JSON payload and posting a single message to an internal chat channel; the documentation does not describe use of a metered or capacity-limited external service, and the threat’s impact is on information integrity rather than unbounded resource consumption, so the bounding requirement does not bear on this threat.

The Event Receiver is a public HTTPS endpoint that accepts deployment events from an external CI platform and triggers the Chat Notifier to post messages, so this threat directly involves an endpoint that accepts events from an external platform and performs state-changing work based on them.

The Event Receiver does not verify the authenticity of inbound events at all and instead accepts any well-formed JSON delivery, so the precondition for this requirement—that authenticity is verified but delivery uniqueness is not—does not hold, and the replay-handling requirement is not yet applicable to this threat.
